title: Formação de palavras
theme: Prefixes (un-, dis-, mis-, pre-, over-, under-, re-), suffixes (-tion, -ment, -ness, -ity, -able, -ise), compounds (closed/hyphenated/open), conversion (noun ↔ verb), nuanced word families
goal: Student decodes and produces new words systematically — using prefixes and suffixes deliberately, recognising compounds, and converting parts of speech with awareness.
connects_to: M17 (Elipse e substituição) — moves from word-level to clause-level economy.
module_chunks: un- / dis- / in- / im- / il- / ir- (negation prefixes)
conversion (email v., google v., friend v., gift v.)

units.title: Negation prefixes
units.grammar_focus: Negation prefixes (un-, dis-, in-, im-, il-, ir-, non-) and which root each takes
units.real_life_context: You form negatives reliably — knowing which prefix attaches to which root and avoiding non-words.

grammar.explanation: "Irresponsible" — "ir-" prefix attaches to roots beginning with "r" (irregular, irrelevant, irreversible). The "in-" prefix has phonological allomorphs: il- before "l" (illegal), im- before "p"/"m"/"b" (impossible, immortal, imbalance), ir- before "r" (irregular), in- elsewhere (incorrect).

"Disagree" — "dis-" prefix indicates opposition or reversal of action. "Dis-" verbs are usually opposite actions (disprove, dismantle, disconnect). "Un-" tends to attach to adjectives (unhappy, untidy), though it works for some verbs too (undo, unpack).
"Illogical" — "il-" attaches to "l-" roots (illegal, illiterate, illogical). The "in-" prefix family's allomorphs follow assimilation: easier to pronounce "il-l" than "in-l".

"Unresponsible" isn't a word. "Responsible" takes "ir-" (root begins with "r"). Many C2 learners default to "un-" because it's the most familiar negation prefix. Lexical memory matters: each word fixes its own negation pattern.

grammar.passage: The audit's findings were unflinching. The decisions had been irresponsible, the reporting illegal, and the executive's denials immoral. Several mid-level managers, who had felt powerless to disagree, were now offered immunity in exchange for testimony. The CEO, displaying the unrepentant tone of someone unprepared for consequences, dismissed the report as illegitimate.
grammar.question: How does the passage describe the CEO's reaction?
grammar.answer: he dismissed the report as illegitimate (and showed an unrepentant tone)
grammar.explanation: Eight negation prefixes in three sentences: unflinching (un-), irresponsible (ir-), illegal (il-), immoral (im-), powerless (-less suffix, not prefix but contrast), unrepentant (un-), unprepared (un-), illegitimate (il-). Each prefix correctly chosen by root.

units.title: Suffixes for nouns
units.real_life_context: You convert verbs and adjectives into abstract nouns — essential for academic and analytic writing.

grammar.explanation: "Decide" → "decision" (-sion suffix). Common verb-to-noun patterns: -sion (decide → decision), -tion (create → creation), -ment (develop → development), -ance/-ence (perform → performance, prefer → preference). Each verb fixes its own noun form.

Adjective → noun via "-ness". Pattern: "happy" → "happiness", "kind" → "kindness", "dark" → "darkness". Note: "y" changes to "i" before "-ness". The "-ness" suffix is one of the most productive in English — almost any adjective can take it.

"Manage" → "management" via "-ment". The "-ment" suffix produces abstract nouns from verbs (achieve → achievement, develop → development, judge → judgment, agree → agreement). Common in academic and business writing.

"Honest" → "honesty" (not "honestness"). Irregular noun formation. Many adjectives form nouns with "-ty" or "-ity" instead of "-ness": "honest → honesty", "able → ability", "sincere → sincerity". Memorising these patterns is part of C2 mastery.

grammar.passage: The institution's annual report read like a study in formal abstraction. 'Development continued across all departments. Recognition of contribution increased measurably. Leadership demonstrated greater accountability. Membership numbers held steady. The relationship between governance and execution improved markedly. The organisation's overall maturity is now beyond question.'
grammar.question: How many abstract nouns appear in the passage?
grammar.answer: at least eight (development, recognition, contribution, leadership, accountability, membership, relationship, governance, execution, organisation, maturity)
grammar.explanation: The passage is built almost entirely on abstract nouns — typical of corporate/academic register. Suffixes used: -ment, -tion, -ship, -ity, -ance, -ence. Nominal density is a marker of formal English.

units.title: Suffixes for adjectives and verbs
units.real_life_context: You convert nouns and verbs into adjectives, or nouns/adjectives into verbs — flexibly.

grammar.explanation: "Rely" → "reliable" (-able suffix, capability). Note spelling: "y" → "i" before "-able". "-able" attaches to verbs to form adjectives meaning "can be X-ed" or "characterised by X". Examples: drinkable, washable, manageable, predictable.

"Modern" → "modernise/modernize" (-ise/-ize, "to make X"). British "-ise", American "-ize". Pattern: adjective + -ise = verb. Other examples: standardise, prioritise, normalise, customise. Very productive suffix in C2 vocabulary.
"Danger" → "dangerous" (-ous, "full of, characterised by"). Pattern: noun + -ous = adjective. Examples: famous, mysterious, courageous, generous, glorious. Often Latinate roots.

"Comprehend" → "comprehensible" (-ible suffix; Latin roots tend to take -ible while Germanic roots take -able). Negation = "in-" + "comprehensible" = "incomprehensible". Not "uncomprehensible" — wrong prefix and wrong suffix combination.

grammar.passage: The architect's brief was unusually demanding. The building had to be beautiful but practical, ambitious but affordable, modern but respectful of its context. It had to be simultaneously accessible, sustainable, and adaptable to uses we could not yet predict. We were asked, in short, to standardise innovation — a paradox if there ever was one.
grammar.question: What paradox does the architect identify?
grammar.explanation: Many derived adjectives: beautiful (-ful), practical (-ical), ambitious (-ous), affordable (-able), respectful (-ful), accessible (-ible), sustainable (-able), adaptable (-able). Verb: standardise (-ise). Word-formation density is C2-typical.

listening_speaking.text: They want to modernise the system.

units.title: Compounds
units.grammar_focus: Compounds — closed (lighthouse), hyphenated (well-known), open (high school) — and the rules for each
units.real_life_context: You write compounds with the right spacing — knowing when to close, hyphenate, or leave open.

grammar.explanation: Many compounds are "closed" — written as one word. Examples: lighthouse, smartphone, software, breakfast, sunlight, classroom, weekend. These have lost the boundary because the meaning has become unified. Closed compounds are the most lexicalised.

"Well-known" is hyphenated when it modifies a noun ("a well-known author"). When it follows the noun and acts as a predicate, no hyphen needed ("the author is well known"). Hyphenation rules depend on position.

grammar.hint: Common open compound for upper secondary education
grammar.explanation: "High school" is an open compound — two words but functioning as one concept. Other open compounds: ice cream, post office, real estate, peanut butter. The decision between open and closed often relates to age and frequency in the language.

grammar.sentence: She is an well known author.
grammar.hint: Hyphenate before the noun, use "a" not "an" (consonant sound)
grammar.explanation: "Well known" → "well-known" when before noun. "An" is wrong because "well" begins with the consonant "w". The hyphenation makes the compound function as a single adjective.

grammar.passage: The newspaper headline was, as always, a study in compound forms. 'WELL-KNOWN LIGHTHOUSE KEEPER MAKES POST OFFICE PEACE WITH LONG-LOST HALF-SISTER'. The reader was momentarily stunned: a closed compound (lighthouse), an open one (post office), two hyphenated ones (well-known, half-sister, long-lost) — and a sentence that managed to be charming despite saying almost nothing concrete.
grammar.question: How many compound forms can you identify in the headline?
grammar.answer: at least five — well-known (hyphenated), lighthouse (closed), post office (open), long-lost (hyphenated), half-sister (hyphenated)
grammar.explanation: Five compounds in one headline: one closed (lighthouse), one open (post office), three hyphenated (well-known, long-lost, half-sister). C2 awareness includes recognising the spacing decisions native writers make instinctively.

listening_speaking.text: The lighthouse keeper has lived there forty years.
I went to high school in Rio.
The author is well known in literary circles.

units.title: Conversion
units.grammar_focus: Conversion (zero derivation) — noun ↔ verb without affix change (email, google, friend, gift, message, text)
units.real_life_context: You convert nouns to verbs (and vice versa) fluidly — typical of modern English, especially tech and social vocabulary.

grammar.explanation: Conversion (zero derivation) — using a noun as a verb without changing form. "Email" was originally a noun (electronic mail); now "to email" is fully accepted as a verb. Many modern English verbs come from this process: to google, to text, to message, to friend, to gift.

"Google" became a verb (to google = to search online). The noun form refers to either the company (Google) or — in informal usage — "a google search" or simply "a search". Brand names becoming verbs is a common conversion path in modern English.
"Message" works as both noun and verb. "Did you message him?" — verb form, identical spelling. Native speakers do this automatically. C2 fluency includes the ease of using such conversions.

grammar.hint: "Message" can stand alone as a verb
grammar.answer: I will message him later. (or: I will send him a message later.)
grammar.explanation: "Sendmessage" isn't a word. Either use "message" alone (verb conversion) or "send + him + a message" (noun usage). The modern conversion makes "message" enough on its own.

grammar.passage: The verbs in the office had quietly evolved. 'Did you slack him?' someone asked. 'Yes, but he hasn't pinged back.' 'Try emailing — or just text.' 'I friended him on the new platform last week, so maybe message there.' Five years ago, none of those verbs existed in their current form. Now they were grammar.
grammar.question: How many conversion-verbs appear in the passage?
grammar.answer: at least five — slack, ping, email, text, friend, message (all converted from nouns or names to verbs)
grammar.explanation: Modern English aggressively converts nouns to verbs: slack (the app) → to slack, ping → to ping, email → to email, text → to text, friend (noun) → to friend (verb). C2 awareness includes recognising and producing these conversions.

listening_speaking.text: I friended her on the new platform.

cross_unit_consolidation: Choose the right negation prefix (un-, in-/im-/il-/ir-, dis-, mis-, non-) for each root
Form abstract nouns from verbs and adjectives (decision, management, happiness, ability, partnership)
Form adjectives from verbs and nouns (reliable, dangerous, sustainable, comprehensible)
Form verbs from adjectives or nouns (modernise, simplify, standardise, harden)
Recognise and produce closed compounds (lighthouse, smartphone), hyphenated compounds (well-known, state-of-the-art before noun), and open compounds (high school, post office)
Apply the position-dependent hyphenation rule (hyphenated before noun, open after noun)
Convert nouns to verbs naturally (email, message, google, friend, gift, screenshot)
Spell irregular forms correctly (honesty not "honestness", ability not "ableness")
